description: Tyler's loudest, messiest swing: blown-out punk-rap noise crashes into lush, jazzy soul suites and string-drenched daydreams. A chaotic, candy-colored sugar rush that flips between screaming distortion and sweet Stevie Wonder-inspired chords.
sound: Self-produced and deliberately overdriven, mixing distorted, clipping drums and grinding guitars (the title track nods toward Death Grips-style noise) with N.E.R.D-indebted synth funk, jazz chords, live strings and soul vocal harmonies. Tracks often turn into multi-part suites that swerve from aggression to lounge smoothness. Tyler's baritone raps are frequently buried in the mix, while hooks come from soul and R&B singers. Energy veers wildly from frantic and abrasive to lazy and summery.
themes: critique of gang culture and rap consumerism
context: Tyler's fourth album, released on Odd Future Records, was produced entirely by him and inspired heavily by Stevie Wonder and N.E.R.D; its strings were recorded at Hans Zimmer's studio. It debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 but drew mixed-to-positive reviews, many critics calling it cluttered and badly mixed. Tyler later called it 'the music I've always wanted to make' and issued an instrumentals edition in 2018, and it has since gained a cult following as the bridge to his later work.

description: A sun-bleached, flower-strewn coming-of-age record where Tyler trades shock value for loneliness, longing and quiet confession. Warm neo-soul chords, sweeping strings and car-window daydreams make it feel like a long, lazy summer spent staring at clouds.
sound: A blend of hip-hop, jazz rap and neo-soul built on lush synth pads, jazzy electric piano, live guitar (much of it by Austin Feinstein), strings and layered vocal harmonies, with Pharrell and Max Martin cited as influences. Tyler keeps his verses short so guest singers and arrangements breathe. Mostly mid-tempo and mellow, punctuated by a few heavy, horror-movie bangers like 'Who Dat Boy' and the warped-accordion 'I Ain't Got Time!'.
settings: summer drive with the windows down
context: Tyler's fifth album and first on Columbia was his most personal yet, deliberately reacting against the impersonal Cherry Bomb; lyrics on 'Garden Shed' and 'I Ain't Got Time!' were widely read as him coming out. It debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, earned widespread acclaim (Pitchfork Best New Music) and a Best Rap Album Grammy nomination, and is regarded as his artistic breakthrough and one of the best albums of the 2010s.

description: A fuzzy, synth-soaked heartbreak opera in which Tyler, wig and suit on, falls hard for a man still tied to his ex. It moves from giddy infatuation to jealousy, obsession and a bruised, graceful goodbye.
sound: A synth-heavy mix of neo-soul, R&B, funk, pop and hip-hop, with distorted analog synths, crunchy bass, warm soul samples and deliberately low-mixed, pitch-shifted, lo-fi vocals. Tyler sings more than he raps, using choir-like harmonies and fuzzed-out textures, and Jerrod Carmichael narrates between songs. Tempos range from blown-out, thumping intensity ('Igor's Theme', 'What's Good') to tender ballads ('Earfquake', 'Are We Still Friends?').
context: Recorded mostly in California between 2017 and 2019 (with sessions at Lake Como and in Atlanta); 'Earfquake' was originally written for Justin Bieber and Rihanna and became Tyler's highest-charting single at the time (No. 13). Igor debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 165,000 units, his first chart-topper, and won Best Rap Album at the 2020 Grammys, which Tyler criticized for boxing his genre-blurring work into rap. It is widely considered one of his defining records.

description: Tyler becomes 'Sir Baudelaire,' a jet-setting rap aristocrat with a passport, a Rolls-Royce and a forbidden crush, while DJ Drama hollers over the beats. Braggadocious mixtape energy and lavish travel fantasies give way to a raw, painful love story.
sound: Framed like one of DJ Drama's Gangsta Grillz mixtapes, with Drama's ad-libbed shout-outs over hard, sample-heavy boom-bap and soulful loops. Tyler raps harder and more confidently than on Igor while still weaving in synth-pop, bossa nova, jazz flute, reggae and lush soul balladry, often switching styles mid-song. Production is dense, cinematic and stereo-panned for headphones; energy moves from swaggering bangers ('Lumberjack', 'Juggernaut') to the 10-minute two-part 'Sweet / I Thought You Wanted to Dance' and the confessional 'Wilshire'.
standoutTracks: Sweet / I Thought You Wanted to Dance
themes: forbidden love for a friend's partner
context: Rolled out with billboards bearing a real phone number, the album draws on DJ Drama's 2000s mixtape series and features a 'Tyler Baudelaire' ID card cover inspired by early-1900s passports. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 169,000 units, later set the record for the largest vinyl sales week for a hip-hop album, and won Best Rap Album at the 2022 Grammys. Critics hailed it as a culmination of his career; a 2023 deluxe, The Estate Sale, added outtakes.

description: A masked, military-green confession booth, narrated by Tyler's mother, in which a man in his thirties wrestles with fame, paranoia, fatherhood and commitment. Marching-band stomps and jazzy soul give way to raw self-examination.
sound: Primarily hip-hop, R&B and jazz with eclectic instrumentation: whispered intros building into marching-band and military-cadence drums, warm neo-soul chords and synth arrangements echoing Cherry Bomb and Flower Boy, plus Zambian rock samples on 'Noid' and James Brown samples on 'Sticky'. Songs often shift sound completely within a few minutes. Spoken passages from his mother, Bonita Smith, tie the sequence together; energy ranges from stomping bangers to tender, confessional ballads.
themes: paranoia about fame and parasocial fans
fatherhood, pregnancy scares and an absent father
context: Built around things his mother told him as a child, the album was released on a Monday at 6 a.m. ET as a statement against the Friday release standard. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 299,000 units, his biggest opening, and gave him his first Hot 100 top 10s ('St. Chroma', 'Noid', 'Sticky'). Critics called it his 'therapy record'; it earned Album of the Year and Best Rap Album nominations at the 2026 Grammys and won Best Album Cover.

description: A sweaty, 28-minute dance party with no concept and no deep lore: just Tyler talking big, flexing and begging you to move. Rap house, Miami bass, New Orleans bounce and jungle, made to be played at full volume with your phone in your pocket.
sound: Described as rap house, dance, funk and techno, the album is built on four-on-the-floor kicks, vocoder-laced funk, booty-bass and Miami/Atlanta bass rhythms, New Orleans bounce, and a jungle break that flips his own 'Cherry Bomb'. Samples include Busta Rhymes' 'Pass the Courvoisier, Part II', Ray Parker Jr.'s Raydio and Memphis rap (Tommy Wright III). Tyler raps with loose, smack-talking swagger over relentlessly upbeat, high-BPM grooves, with a few sweeter R&B moments.
themes: dancing without fear of being filmed
context: Recorded largely on the road during Chromakopia: The World Tour and announced only days before release, it is Tyler's shortest album (about 28 minutes, 10 tracks). He said it was 'not made for sitting still' and held a phone-free listening party at Hollywood Forever Cemetery. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 197,000 units, his fourth straight chart-topper, drew generally favorable reviews as a fun, low-stakes palate cleanser, and was nominated for Best Alternative Music Album at the 2026 Grammys.

description: A hazy, drifting meditation on love, memory, youth and loss, sung over spare guitars, organs and silence. Frank Ocean's long-awaited masterpiece feels like a sunset drive replayed in fragments, intimate and achingly beautiful.
sound: Avant-soul that stretches R&B into minimalist indie rock, ambient electronica and psychedelia, often with little or no percussion. Songs rest on looping electric and acoustic guitars, church organ and keyboards, with lush Beach Boys-style vocal harmonies, pitch-shifted and varispeed vocals, spoken-word interludes and sudden beat switches (the mid-song flip in 'Nights'). Tempos are slow and languid, and songs drift and change shape rather than building to big choruses.
context: Long teased as 'Boys Don't Cry,' the album was recorded between 2013 and 2016 at Electric Lady, Abbey Road and Henson studios and released independently as an Apple exclusive the day after the visual album Endless, alongside a free magazine. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 276,000 units and was not submitted for the Grammys by Ocean. Time named it 2016's best album, Pitchfork named it the best album of the 2010s, and Rolling Stone ranks it among the 500 greatest albums of all time.

description: A smoky, psychedelic trip through Harlem swagger, acid haze and grief, made in the shadow of A$AP Yams' death. Rocky floats between druggy, cloud-rap guitar dreams, gospel-tinged gloom and high-fashion flexing.
sound: Psychedelic hip-hop mixing woozy, reverb-drenched guitars, gospel and soul samples, '60s rock touches and Houston chopped-and-screwed DNA, overseen by Danger Mouse and Hector Delgado. Rocky switches between laid-back drawls, pitched-down vocals and sung melodies, with London street performer Joe Fox adding guitar and hooks throughout. Mostly mid-to-slow tempo and hazy, with brighter moments like the Rod Stewart-sampling 'Everyday' and the bouncy 'Electric Body'.
context: Made after the sudden death of mentor and A$AP Mob founder A$AP Yams in January 2015, who is credited as an executive producer alongside Danger Mouse, Juicy J and Rocky. It leaked and was released a week early, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 146,000 units, Rocky's second chart-topper, and was later certified double platinum. Reviews were generally positive, praising its expensive, trippy sound while criticizing thin lyrics.

description: Rocky's lab experiment: a jagged, distorted, genre-colliding rap album that throws Moby, grime, Memphis rap, psychedelia and Lauryn Hill into the beaker. Restless and uneven, it ends in Frank Ocean's gorgeous, soulful 'Purity'.
sound: Experimental hip-hop built on deliberately distorted, blown-out production, chopped vocals, noisy electronic and dance textures (Boys Noize), grime (Skepta), Memphis-rap samples, and psychedelic and indie touches (Dev Hynes, FKA Twigs). Songs collide contrasting ideas and often lurch mid-track. Rocky's flows are laid-back and fashion-forward, and energy swings from grimy and menacing to dreamy and soulful.
themes: loyalty and his A$AP Mob roots
context: Rocky said the album was about 'testing new sounds' rather than chasing the charts; it was preceded by the Moby-sampling 'A$AP Forever' and later the Skepta collaboration 'Praise the Lord (Da Shine)'. It debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with 75,000 units and was later certified gold. Reviews were mixed-to-positive: critics admired its ambition and highlights like 'Purity' and 'Fukk Sleep' but found it uneven and unfocused.

description: Travis Scott's dark, cinematic debut is a psychedelic trap carnival, full of Auto-Tuned howls, bruising 808s and towering Mike Dean synths, framed as a T.I.-narrated rodeo. Druggy, nocturnal and huge-sounding, it soundtracks a reckless night that never ends.
sound: Psychedelic, maximalist trap with booming 808s, distorted bass, swirling synths and guitar solos from Mike Dean, abrupt beat switches, and heavily Auto-Tuned, reverb-drenched vocals used as texture. Producers include Metro Boomin, WondaGurl, Frank Dukes, Sonny Digital and Allen Ritter. Energy ranges from mosh-ready bangers ('Antidote', 'Nightcrawler') to woozy, spacey slow burns ('90210', 'Maria I'm Drunk'), with T.I. narration tying the story together.
themes: the struggle to stay on top (the rodeo metaphor)
context: Scott's debut album, released via Grand Hustle and Epic, frames his life as a rodeo he struggles to ride, with T.I. as narrator. Lead single '3500' was followed by 'Antidote', which peaked at No. 16 on the Hot 100, his biggest hit at the time. It debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 with 85,000 units; contemporary reviews were mixed-to-positive (critics praised the production but called him derivative), but it became a cult fan favorite, was certified double platinum in 2024, and set the template for his later blockbusters.

description: Travis Scott's foggy, star-studded second album: syrupy Houston trap soaked in Auto-Tune, reverb and late-night hedonism. A dark, woozy ride from the haunted 'goosebumps' to the sweet pop-trap of 'pick up the phone', it sounds like the hazy after-hours of a party that never ends.
sound: Dark, atmospheric trap built on swarming 808 bass, sluggish half-time drums and gauzy, glittering synth and keyboard layers, mixed with Mike Dean's lush, spacey polish. Scott's voice is drenched in Auto-Tune and effects, functioning more as texture and melody than lyricism, with chant-like hooks and ad-libs. Tempo is mostly slow-to-mid and narcotic, with occasional bouncier moments ('Pick Up the Phone') and a Kid Cudi 'Day 'n' Nite' interpolation on 'Through the Late Night'; samples include Washed Out on 'SDP Interlude'.
settings: headphones in the city at night
context: Released via Grand Hustle/Epic after several delays, it premiered on Scott and Chase B's Beats 1 show Wav Radio. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 88,000 units, Scott's first chart-topper, and was later certified 4x platinum. Reviews were generally favorable (Metacritic 64), praising the lush production while knocking the vapid lyrics; 'Goosebumps' with Kendrick Lamar became one of his signature songs.

description: A psychedelic theme-park ride through Travis Scott's Houston childhood, named after the demolished Six Flags AstroWorld. Full of beat switches, roaring 808s, dreamy detours and superstar cameos, it's his blockbuster: equal parts mosh-pit adrenaline and hazy, starry-eyed trip.
sound: Psychedelic trap and hip-hop with cinematic, constantly shifting production: mid-song beat switches (famously on 'Sicko Mode'), distorted bass, rushing synths, and lush live touches like John Mayer's guitar, Stevie Wonder's harmonica and Thundercat's bass. Tame Impala co-produces the kaleidoscopic 'Skeletons', while 'Coffee Bean' closes on a blissed-out funk guitar. Scott's Auto-Tuned yelps and ad-libs drive high-energy rage moments ('Stargazing', 'No Bystanders') balanced against slower, druggy, dreamlike passages.
themes: spirituality and ego ('Stop Trying to Be God')
context: Recorded 2016–2018 (finished partly in Hawaii) and framed as a sequel to his debut Rodeo, it debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 537,000 units, with all 17 tracks charting on the Hot 100 and 'Sicko Mode' hitting No. 1. It earned a Metacritic 85, was nominated for Best Rap Album at the 61st Grammys, won Album of the Year at the 2019 BET Hip Hop Awards, and is certified 6x platinum. It's widely ranked among the best albums of the 2010s and defines Scott's chaotic live-show persona.

description: Travis Scott's sprawling, grandiose return: a dark, industrial, psychedelic spectacle stuffed with abrupt beat switches, distorted synths and A-list guests from Beyoncé to Playboi Carti. Huge, abrasive and theatrical, it feels like a stadium-sized rave inside a dystopian circus.
sound: Maximalist experimental trap and psychedelic hip-hop with industrial textures, distorted and blown-out bass, ominous synths, and frequent dramatic beat switches; heavily influenced by Kanye West's Yeezus era (West co-produces 'Thank God' and 'Telekinesis'). Ranges from the frantic, chant-driven rage of 'Fein' and the hard-hitting 'Meltdown' to the progressive, sample-heavy 'Hyaena' (Gentle Giant, Funkadelic), the Bon Iver-assisted 'My Eyes' and the ambient James Blake/Metro Boomin closer. Scott's vocals are processed and Auto-Tuned, emphasizing feel and energy over lyrics.
context: Recorded from 2019 onward and released with the companion film Circus Maximus; its planned launch show at the Pyramids of Giza was canceled and replaced by a concert at Rome's Circus Maximus. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 496,000 units, all 19 songs charted on the Hot 100, and it became Scott's first UK No. 1. Critics were divided (Metacritic 67), praising the production but criticizing its cohesion, thin lyrics and heavy debt to Kanye West; 'Fein' became a massive live staple.

description: Playboi Carti's sugar-rush debut: bubbly, glitchy Pi'erre Bourne beats and endlessly looped baby-voiced chants built for teenage mosh pits. Hedonistic, minimalist and weirdly euphoric, it plays like a video game soundtrack for a party that's going off the rails.
sound: Minimalist trap and cloud rap produced mostly by Pi'erre Bourne (15 of 19 tracks): twinkly, video-game-like synth loops, bright melodic fragments and booming 808s. Carti's delivery is ad-lib heavy and 'post-verbal', using repetition, pitched-up 'baby voice' and mumbled chants as rhythmic instruments rather than storytelling. Mid-tempo but kinetic and bouncy, with punk energy borrowed from his live shows; 'Fell in Luv' chops Purity Ring vocals and 'R.I.P.' rides a foreboding Jodeci sample.
context: Recorded in Atlanta between December 2017 and March 2018 and surprise-released on AWGE/Interscope after the SoundCloud single 'Love Hurts', it debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 with 61,000 units and went gold. Reviews were generally favorable (Metacritic 71), with Pitchfork calling it a perversely infectious sugar high. It's now credited as a blueprint for the SoundCloud-era underground and the later rage sound; Rolling Stone ranked it No. 144 among the 250 greatest albums of the 21st century in 2025.

description: Playboi Carti's chaotic vampire-punk opus: 24 tracks of blown-out synths, screamed and squeaked vocals, and gothic rockstar menace. Divisive on release and now a cult classic, it's the defining record of rage rap, pure adrenaline for mosh pits and midnight mayhem.
sound: Experimental hip-hop, rage and trap with punk and electronic influences: distorted, serrated synth leads, blown-out 808s and abrasive, minimal beats from F1lthy, Art Dealer and others, often abandoning verse-chorus structure for chants. Carti's voice swings from raspy, guttural punk yells to an ultra-high 'baby voice' and falsetto, used as an instrument. Mostly fast, frenetic and loud ('Stop Breathing', 'Slay3r', 'New Tank'), with gothic touches like the Bach Toccata organ on 'Vamp Anthem' and softer, nostalgic moments ('Sky', 'Place', the Bon Iver-sampling closer 'F33l Lik3 Dyin'). Compared often to Kanye West's Yeezus.
context: Recorded largely alone in Atlanta during late-night sessions and finished with executive producer Kanye West in Wyoming and Calabasas, it was released on Christmas Day 2020 after years of delay. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 100,000 units (Carti's first chart-topper) and went gold. Initially polarizing, it was later hailed as the album that defined the rage subgenre and shaped artists like Yeat and Ken Carson; Pitchfork ranked it No. 2 among the best albums of the 2020s so far (2024).

description: After a four-year wait, Playboi Carti's sprawling 30-track MUSIC swaps the baby voice for a deep, raspy growl over hard-hitting Atlanta trap. Loud, braggadocious and packed with Travis Scott, Kendrick Lamar and the Weeknd, it's a long, relentless rager with a few melodic, moody detours.
sound: Southern hip-hop and trap built on booming 808s, skittering hi-hats and dark synths from Ojivolta, Cardo and F1lthy, with contributions from Metro Boomin, Wheezy, Kanye West and others; critics noted a Hungarian psychedelic sample and chipmunk-soul touches. Carti mostly uses a lower, rougher, more aggressive voice, though he switches registers (a high pitch on 'I Seeeeee You Baby Boi', freestyle on 'HBA'). Energetic bangers ('Pop Out', 'Crush', 'Evil J0rdan') alternate with melodic R&B-leaning cuts ('Rather Lie', 'Backd00r'), plus DJ Swamp Izzo mixtape-style hosting and abrupt transitions.
context: Long-teased under titles like Narcissist and recorded partly in a cave-like Paris studio and DJ Drama's Atlanta studio, it debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 298,000 units, the biggest rap debut of 2025, and all 30 songs entered the Hot 100 (a first for a rapper). Reviews were generally favorable (Metacritic 73), praising production and vocals but citing inconsistency and length. A deluxe, Music – Sorry 4 da Wait, followed on March 25, 2025, and online theories questioned whether some vocals were AI-generated, which Carti reportedly denied.

description: YoungBoy Never Broke Again's raw, haunted debut album: Baton Rouge street rap full of pain, paranoia and violence, sung and shouted with startling emotional urgency. Dark, confessional and menacing, it sounds like a teenager staring down an early grave.
sound: Louisiana street rap and melodic trap with somber piano and synth melodies, heavy 808s and tense, minor-key beats from producers including DJ Swift, CashMoneyAP, Ben Billions, Kenny Beats and Wheezy/TM88. YoungBoy's delivery is intense and emotionally raw, switching between rapid, aggressive bars and pained, melodic half-singing. Energy ranges from menacing, adrenalized cuts ('Diamond Teeth Samurai', which interpolates 'Tha Block Is Hot') to brooding, mournful confessionals ('Overdose', 'Traumatized').
context: His first official studio album on Never Broke Again/Atlantic, pushed from March to April 2018 after a string of mixtapes. It debuted at No. 7 on the Billboard 200 with 43,000 units (his first top-10) and was certified platinum in 2019; lead single 'Outside Today' reached No. 31 on the Hot 100. Critics gave mixed reviews, with Pitchfork describing it as a meditation on violence, conscience and anticipating an early death. A Reloaded edition added tracks with Offset and Lil Uzi Vert.

description: YoungBoy Never Broke Again's chart-topping second album: 21 tracks of emotional, guitar-laced Baton Rouge rap swinging from heartbreak and depression to street threats and fatherhood. Vulnerable and volatile, it's the sound of a young star wrestling with fame, love and danger.
sound: Melodic trap and Southern street rap with moody guitar loops, piano and synth melodies, and booming 808s from producers like TayTayMadeIt, Cheese, Wheezy, JetsonMade, Smash David and Cubeatz. YoungBoy alternates between wounded, melodic half-singing and fast, aggressive, high-energy rapping. Moods swing between tender, aching tracks ('All In', 'Callin' with Snoop Dogg) and menacing street cuts ('Murder Business', 'Dead Trollz'), with playful moments like 'Kacey Talk', which features ad-libs from his young son.
context: Released on Never Broke Again/Atlantic after YoungBoy briefly vowed to stop releasing music amid a dispute with his label, it was expanded from 18 to 21 tracks just before release. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 126,000 units, his third No. 1 in under a year, with nine songs entering the Hot 100. Critics gave it generally positive reviews, with AllMusic praising a new level of versatility and expression; its black-and-white cover drew comparisons to Roddy Ricch's Please Excuse Me for Being Antisocial.

description: Kanye West's messy, sprawling 'gospel album with a whole lot of cursing': soaring choirs and church organs collide with trap, soul samples and raw confession. Manic, holy, funny and paranoid, it swings from spiritual uplift to ego, lust and family strife like a living, unfinished masterpiece.
sound: Intentionally fragmented hip-hop blending gospel (choirs, organ, Kirk Franklin on 'Ultralight Beam'), soul samples, Auto-Tuned melancholy, trap ('Pt. 2' with Desiigner), industrial and avant-pop textures ('Feedback') and house-influenced dance ('Fade'). Production by West with Mike Dean, Noah Goldstein, Rick Rubin, Metro Boomin, Hudson Mohawke, Madlib and others shifts abruptly between moods and tempos, many tracks feeling deliberately unfinished. West's delivery ranges from boastful and comedic to vulnerable and pleading.
context: Recorded 2013–2016 under working titles So Help Me God, Swish and Waves, it premiered at Madison Square Garden during Yeezy Season 3 and was initially a Tidal exclusive; West kept updating songs after release, calling it a 'living breathing changing creative expression.' It became the first album to top the Billboard 200 primarily through streaming and is certified 3x platinum. Reviews were positive (Metacritic 75); it earned five Grammy nominations including Best Rap Album, and the lack of an Album of the Year nod was widely called a snub. The 'Famous' line about Taylor Swift sparked a major controversy.

description: Kanye West and Kid Cudi's short, cathartic team-up: seven tracks of fuzzy psychedelic rock-rap, frantic scatting and hard-won spiritual rebirth. Dark and haunted at first, it climbs toward liberation, a soundtrack for fighting your demons and coming out free.
sound: Psychedelic hip-hop fused with rap rock, fuzzed-out '70s-style guitars, distorted drums, ethereal synths and blurry, dreamlike crescendos, mostly produced by West and Cudi with Mike Dean, Plain Pat and Dot da Genius. West delivers frantic, percussive scatting on 'Feel the Love'; '4th Dimension' samples a vintage Louis Prima Christmas song; 'Cudi Montage' uses a Kurt Cobain sample. Energy moves from abrasive and explosive ('Feel the Love', 'Freeee') to hypnotic and uplifting ('Reborn'), with Cudi's trademark hums and moans throughout.
context: Made after West and Cudi reconciled in late 2016 (following a public falling-out, Cudi's rehab for depression and West's hospitalization), it was the third of West's 'Wyoming Sessions' releases recorded in Jackson Hole, with cover art by Takashi Murakami. It debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 behind Dave Matthews Band and later went gold, with all seven tracks charting and 'Reborn' going platinum. It received universal acclaim (Metacritic 84) and is widely regarded as a cult classic about mental health.

description: Don Toliver's debut under Travis Scott's Cactus Jack: a woozy, psychedelic trip of melodic trap where his elastic, high-pitched croon floats over glossy, spacey beats. Hazy, hook-drunk and quietly euphoric, it feels like the slow-motion glow of an after-party at 3am.
sound: Psychedelic, melodic trap and Houston-rooted hip-hop with lush synth pads, warped keys, rumbling 808s and Mike Dean's spacey mixing and mastering across the whole record. Toliver mostly sings rather than raps, using a nasal, stretchy falsetto-tinged voice layered with Auto-Tune and reverb, building hooks out of drawn-out melodies. Tempos sit mid-paced and bouncy ('After Party', 'No Idea') or drift into slow, druggy haze ('Can't Feel My Legs'), with a short runtime and smooth, cinematic sequencing.
context: Toliver signed to Cactus Jack after his breakout guest spot on Travis Scott's Astroworld, and 'After Party' had been teased in Scott's Netflix documentary Look Mom I Can Fly before release. The album debuted at No. 7 on the Billboard 200 with 44,000 units, his first top-ten album, and was certified platinum by the RIAA in 2023. It drew generally positive reviews, and 'After Party' became his signature hit; a chopped-and-screwed 'Chopnotslop' remix followed in April 2020.

description: Ken Carson's major-label debut on Playboi Carti's Opium: relentless, blown-out rage rap of glitchy synths, pounding 808s and Auto-Tuned yelps. A bratty, hedonistic sugar rush built to recreate the chaos of his mosh-pit live shows.
sound: High-energy rage and plugg-influenced trap with buzzing, glitchy synthesizer leads, distorted 808 drums and pounding bass, executive produced by Playboi Carti with beats from F1lthy, Lil 88 and others. Carson raps in a repetitive, slurred, heavily Auto-Tuned delivery full of ad-libs, often compared to Carti's Whole Lotta Red. Energy is almost uniformly loud and frantic across a long tracklist, with the closer 'The End' a rare mellow, Auto-Tune-free sung moment.
context: Released through Opium and Interscope a year after his debut Project X, X was Carson's first album to enter the Billboard 200, debuting at No. 115. Critics were mixed, faulting its repetitiveness and its closeness to Carti's sound, but 'Freestyle 2' became a TikTok dance trend and fan favorite, later certified Platinum. Carson toured it on the X-Man Tour with Destroy Lonely, and a five-track deluxe, Xtended, arrived that October.

description: Ken Carson's breakout: maximalist, blown-out rage rap where crunchy, glitchy synth walls, horror-movie atmosphere and deafening 808s collide. Hedonistic and menacing with flashes of angst, it sounds like a strobe-lit vampire rave inside a corrupted video file.
sound: Maximalist rage and futuristic trap with digitized, crunchy synth arpeggios, distorted organ-like basslines, glitch effects and an intentionally loud, muddy mix centered on Carson's blunt, slurred, Auto-Tuned delivery. Producers including F1lthy, Lil 88, Star Boy, Outtatown and TM88 layer dense walls of sound with occasional delicate, Kraftwerk-like melodies. Pacing is tighter than X, staying at high intensity, with 'I Need U' a buzzing synth love song and horror and internet 'creepypasta' imagery coloring titles and textures.
settings: late-night drive with the bass up
context: After X's poor reviews, Carson recorded nightly, even on tour, often playing horror films in the studio; sample-clearance issues pushed the release from July to October 2023. It debuted at No. 11 on the Billboard 200 with about 48,000 units, became his breakout and was certified Platinum in 2025, with 'Overseas' his first Hot 100 entry. It drew the best reviews of his career, appearing on year-end lists from Complex, The Washington Post and Rolling Stone, and Pitchfork ranked it among the best albums of the 2020s so far.

description: Lil Uzi Vert's long-awaited sci-fi epic: an hour of hyperactive, video-game-bright trap told through alien abduction and three alter egos. Flex-heavy, futuristic and endlessly bouncy, with a vein of lovesick melancholy beneath the lasers.
sound: Futuristic melodic trap with glitchy synths, booming 808s, laser and arcade sound effects and pinball samples, largely produced by Philly's Working on Dying collective and others. Uzi switches between rapid-fire rapping, melodic crooning and high-pitched ad-libs, sequenced in three six-song arcs (Baby Pluto, Renji, Uzi) that move from aggressive flexing to vulnerable introspection to cosmic reflection. Energy is mostly fast and frenetic, with bonus tracks 'Futsal Shuffle 2020' (a dance record) and 'That Way' (interpolating the Backstreet Boys).
context: After years of label delays, cryptic teases and a scrapped Heaven's Gate-inspired cover, Uzi surprise-released Eternal Atake a week early, followed by the deluxe Lil Uzi Vert vs. the World 2. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 288,000 units and 400 million streams, while 'Baby Pluto', 'Lo Mein' and 'Silly Watch' all debuted in the Hot 100 top ten. Critics widely called it Uzi's best work (Metacritic 84), and it ranked as the seventh best-selling album of 2020 in the US.

description: Steve Lacy's breakup album: warm, sticky-sweet bedroom funk and indie rock where jangly guitars, falsetto and lo-fi grooves wrap around messy feelings. Flirty, petty, playful and tender, like a hot summer afternoon spent half-heartbroken.
sound: A blend of indie rock, alternative R&B, funk, jazz and psychedelic soul, around 90% produced by Lacy himself, with contributions from DJ Dahi and Matt Martians. Built on Lacy's clean, chorus-heavy guitar, loose bass grooves and live-sounding drums, with organ, synths and gospel-tinged background vocals. Vocals swing between conversational singing, falsetto and impish ad-libs; the tempo is relaxed and grooving, with sudden turns (the beat switch in 'Bad Habit') and jam-session spontaneity over a concise 10-track runtime.
context: Lacy's major-label debut on RCA, made as a story of 'coming into himself' after a breakup, followed 2019's Apollo XXI. 'Bad Habit' became his first Hot 100 entry and a No. 1 single, while the album peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard 200 and topped the Top Rock Albums chart. Critics praised its funky, jam-session warmth (Metacritic 80), and it won the Grammy for Best Progressive R&B Album.

description: Brent Faiyaz's cinematic, nocturnal R&B confession: silky falsetto over sparse, smoky beats, telling a story of fame, vice and toxic love. Seductive and self-destructive at once, with tense relationship skits that turn the late-night romance sour.
sound: Moody, minimal alternative R&B with nocturnal, often sparse production: muted drums, warm keys, vintage soul textures and moments with almost no percussion ('Ghetto Gatsby'). Produced mainly by Faiyaz and Jordan Ware, with help from The Neptunes, No I.D., Raphael Saadiq, DJ Dahi and Jake One. Faiyaz's smooth, airy tenor and falsetto carry effortless hooks at slow-to-mid tempos, while spoken skits and a long intro give a film-like narrative structure.
themes: an unplanned pregnancy and relationship conflict
context: Recorded across New York, Atlanta, Los Angeles and the Bahamas over roughly two years, with lead single 'Dead Man Walking' (2020) written in reaction to George Floyd's murder, the album frames fame as a post-pandemic 'wasteland'. Released through his own Lost Kids imprint, it debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 with 88,000 units and was certified Platinum in 2023. Reviews were generally favorable (Metacritic 73), praising its vocals and smooth production while some found the skits and length excessive.

description: Daniel Caesar's restless third album: gospel-rooted R&B stretched into folk, soft rock and psychedelic soul. Intimate, searching and quietly sensual, it sits in the hazy space between longing, self-doubt and grown-up regret.
sound: Warm, mellow alternative R&B that wanders into folk, soft rock, reggae-tinged and experimental textures, much of it built by Caesar himself on guitar, bass and drums with producer Sir Dylan. Instrumentation is organic and hazy: soft drum programming, live bass, strings, synth bass and woozy guitar, with contributions from BadBadNotGood, Raphael Saadiq and Mark Ronson. Caesar's gentle, falsetto-laced croon stays front and center at slow, drifting tempos, with brief vignettes alongside full ballads.
context: Recorded largely by Caesar himself after pandemic quarantine, Never Enough was his first album for Republic and deliberately reached beyond R&B toward folk and country influences. It debuted at No. 14 on the Billboard 200 and No. 8 in Canada. Reviews were generally positive (Metacritic 72); it was shortlisted for the 2023 Polaris Music Prize and won the Juno Award for Contemporary R&B/Soul Recording of the Year in 2024.

description: Kendrick Lamar's sprawling masterpiece: jazz, funk, soul and spoken word woven into a furious, soul-searching portrait of Black America. Defiant, anguished and ultimately hopeful, it moves from depression and survivor's guilt to the protest anthem 'Alright'.
sound: Hip-hop fused with free jazz, P-Funk, G-funk, soul and spoken-word poetry, played by the West Coast Get Down circle including Thundercat, Terrace Martin, Kamasi Washington and Robert Glasper, with Flying Lotus, Sounwave and Pharrell among the producers. Expect live bass, wailing saxophones, wah-wah guitars, Isley Brothers and Boris Gardiner samples, and George Clinton cameos. Lamar shifts voices constantly, from rapid jazz-cadence rapping and slurred, drunken crying ('U') to recurring poem recitations, ending in a 12-minute 'conversation' with Tupac. The energy swings from funky strut ('King Kunta') to dense, chaotic collage.
themes: fame, temptation and exploitation by the industry
context: Inspired by a trip to South Africa including Mandela's Robben Island cell, Lamar scrapped earlier material and wrote parts of 'Mortal Man' on Kanye West's Yeezus Tour; the album leaked out a week early via a label error. It debuted at No. 1 in the US (324,000 copies) and UK, won the Grammy for Best Rap Album, and 'Alright' became a rallying cry of the Black Lives Matter movement. With a Metacritic score of 96, it topped countless 2015 and decade-end lists and ranked No. 19 on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.

description: Kendrick Lamar's surprise victory lap after the Drake war: a lean, speaker-rattling love letter to West Coast rap, bouncing between hyphy menace, G-funk swagger and tender SZA duets. Confrontational, confident and very Los Angeles.
sound: West Coast hip-hop drawing on classic G-funk, bounce and contemporary LA street rap, produced mainly by Lamar with Sounwave and Jack Antonoff, plus Mustard, Sean Momberger and Kamasi Washington. Expect knocking basslines, clipped strings and sudden horn-blasting beat switches ('TV Off'), soulful samples (Luther Vandross on 'Luther', SWV on 'Heart Pt. 6'), and mariachi singer Deyra Barrera framing the album. Lamar raps in shapeshifting, often manic voices and shrieks; the 44-minute runtime is mostly punchy and uptempo, with warmer, romantic breaks.
themes: West Coast and Los Angeles pride
settings: cruising LA streets with the windows down
context: Named after the 1987 Buick GNX and Lamar's first album after leaving TDE and Aftermath, it was surprise-released with no announcement following his 2024 feud with Drake. It debuted at No. 1 with 319,000 units, with all 12 songs entering the Hot 100 and 'Squabble Up' and 'Luther' reaching No. 1; Lamar performed its songs at the record-setting Super Bowl LIX halftime show. Critics acclaimed it (Metacritic 87), and it won the Grammy for Best Rap Album, with 'Luther' winning Record of the Year and 'TV Off' Best Rap Song.

description: Metro Boomin's cinematic, superhero-themed trap blockbuster: dark, orchestral beats, all-star guests and Morgan Freeman narration. Ominous and grand, it swings from villainous menace to sleek late-night R&B, like a gangster film scored for arenas.
sound: Psychedelic, cinematic trap with dark piano and string arrangements, choir, brass, heavy 808s and moody synth atmospheres, mixed by Metro with orchestral contributions from Johan Lenox and Peter Lee Johnson. Samples range from Kanye West's 'So Appalled' to Peabo Bryson and a Mario Winans 'I Don't Wanna Know' reworking on 'Creepin''. Guests trade rapping and Auto-Tuned singing at mostly mid, head-nodding tempos, with spoken narration by Morgan Freeman and ASAP Rocky tying the hero/villain concept together.
context: The sequel to 2018's Not All Heroes Wear Capes, it was dedicated to Metro's late mother and delayed a month by sample clearances; its cover nods to Pink Floyd's Wish You Were Here. It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 185,000 units, Metro's third No. 1, was certified Platinum in 2023, and 'Creepin'' with the Weeknd and 21 Savage became a major hit. Reviews were generally favorable (Metacritic 73), praising its world-building and star power while noting it occasionally crams in too much.
